questions.prompt: On a single-core MCU, the main loop does `count = count + 1` and the audio callback (an interrupt) does `count = count - 1` on the same `volatile int count`. Over time the count drifts. Why?

options.text: Integer overflow
options.explanation: Overflow would cause a large jump at the limit, not a slow random drift.

options.text: The compiler caches `count` in a register
options.explanation: volatile prevents caching, so this is not the cause here.

options.text: Read-modify-write is three steps; if the callback interrupts between the main loop's read and write, the main loop then writes back a stale value and erases the callback's decrement
options.explanation: Correct. That is a lost update. volatile does not make the sequence indivisible; use an atomic fetch-add, or have each side own its own counter.

options.text: The callback runs twice per block
options.explanation: It runs once per block; frequency is not the issue.

questions.workedExample:
```
main: r = count      (r = 5)
  -- interrupt --
cb:   count = count-1 (now 4)
  -- return --
main: count = r + 1  (6!)
```

Expected 5, got 6: the decrement vanished. A design with one writer per variable avoids the problem entirely.

link.title: Why volatile should not be used — Linux kernel docs

questions.prompt: A preset change must update ten parameters together so the callback never renders a block with a mix of old and new values. Which approach is safe and never makes the callback wait?

options.text: Ten separate atomics written in sequence by the main loop
options.explanation: Each is safe individually, but the callback can run between writes and see five new and five old.

options.text: Wrap the ten writes in a mutex that the callback also locks
options.explanation: The callback would wait if the main loop held the lock: forbidden in real-time code.

options.text: Write the ten values into a plain struct and set a volatile flag
options.explanation: volatile does not order the struct writes before the flag (see the reordering problem).

options.text: Send the whole preset as one queued message, or use double buffering with atomic publication and an acknowledgement before reusing the old buffer
options.explanation: Correct. Complete sets stay immutable while the callback reads them; publication alone does not make reuse safe.

questions.workedExample: Prefer a bounded SPSC queue for the whole preset. For double buffering, permit only one unacknowledged publication. Publish index plus generation with release ordering. The callback acquire-loads that publication and, after its last read of the old set, release-stores the adopted generation as acknowledgement. Only after acquiring that exact acknowledgement may the producer refill the old set. A block-start counter can change before adoption, so it is insufficient. The callback never waits.

questions.prompt: You port your synth from a single-core MCU to a multi-core Raspberry Pi, where the control thread and audio thread run simultaneously. Which statements hold? Select all that apply.

options.text: Atomics with release/acquire ordering remain correct, because they also provide the memory barriers multi-core CPUs need
options.explanation: Correct. That is one reason to write atomics even on a single-core MCU.

options.text: Code relying on 'an aligned 32-bit store is one instruction' plus volatile, without atomics, may now fail through hardware reordering between cores
options.explanation: Correct. Multi-core processors can make writes visible to other cores in a different order unless barriers are used.

options.text: Disabling interrupts in the control thread is a valid way to stop the audio thread running
options.explanation: On a multi-core OS, the audio thread may be on another core; disabling local interrupts (if even permitted) does not stop it.

options.text: A lock-free SPSC ring buffer with correct orderings still works between the two threads
options.explanation: Correct. SPSC queues are a standard real-time inter-thread mechanism on desktop and Linux audio too.

questions.workedExample:
What changes on multi-core:

1. True parallelism: both sides run at once.
2. Each core may see the other's writes in a different order without barriers.
3. Interrupt masking is per-core and usually unavailable to user programs.

Patterns built on atomics with explicit ordering survive the port; patterns built on single-core assumptions do not.

lessons.title: Comparing synth platforms
lessons.summary: A method for evaluating a Daisy Seed, a Teensy 4.x with its audio adaptor and a Raspberry Pi with an audio HAT against the project's own criteria, using only official documentation, with model, revision and date recorded. A comparison approach, not a recommendation.
lessons.body:
The diy-synth project deliberately leaves the board open. This lesson does not choose one. It gives you a repeatable method for comparing candidates, demonstrates it with facts taken only from the manufacturers' current documentation, and shows where the evidence runs out.

> [!warning] Re-verify before buying
> Every product fact below was checked on **2026-10-04** against the named official source and model or revision. Boards change revision, codecs get substituted (the Daisy Seed has had three), and products move between manufacturers. Treat this lesson as a snapshot. Re-check each fact against the current official page before you spend money, and record your own check date.

## Step 1: write the criteria before looking at boards

Looking at spec sheets first makes the biggest numbers feel important. Start from the project instead. The project brief and the hardware-options checklist give these criteria:

**Must-haves** (pass/fail):

- Audio output suitable for an audio interface's line input.
- A control connection an external device (the Digitakt) can drive.
- Enough inputs for the planned buttons and knobs.
- A C++ toolchain that works on the development computer.
- A documented way to flash, and to recover a broken board.
- Low-voltage power only.

**Weighted criteria** (scored):

- Beginner documentation and working audio examples.
- Debugging workflow and extra equipment needed.
- CPU, RAM and flash headroom for the intended synth.
- Total prototype cost: board plus audio board, MIDI circuit, power, cables, tools.
- Soldering and construction effort.
- Availability, revision stability, maintenance.
- Fit with the learning goals (C++, DSP, embedded).

Decide the weights *before* scoring, and write down why.

## Step 2: define exact configurations

"Teensy" is not a configuration. Compare complete, buildable systems:

| Label | Configuration |
|---|---|
| A | Daisy Seed, Rev 7 |
| B | Teensy 4.1 + audio adaptor Rev D2 |
| C | Raspberry Pi 5 + Raspberry Pi DAC+ |

Each still needs a DIN MIDI interface circuit (or another agreed control link), power, cables, and possibly a debug probe. List those per configuration; they are part of the cost and the build effort. (Pi alternatives include the DAC Pro or the Codec Zero, which differ in outputs and inputs.)

## Step 3: gather evidence from official sources only

Below is what the official sources state, checked 2026-10-04.

### A: Daisy Seed (Rev 7)

Sources: Electro-Smith Daisy Seed page and datasheet v1.2.0 (18 March 2026); libDaisy documentation.

- Arm Cortex-M7 at 480 MHz; 64 MB SDRAM; 8 MB flash (external QSPI; internal flash is 128 KB).
- 96 kHz / 24-bit stereo audio in and out (PCM3060 codec on Rev 7); line-level output, 0 dBFS at 1 V RMS, 100 Ω output impedance.
- 31 GPIO, 12 × 16-bit ADC inputs, 2 × 12-bit DAC outputs; SPI, UART, I2S, I2C.
- Micro USB port, plus USB pins for OTG host and device.
- Power: VIN 5–17 V. Most GPIO 5 V tolerant; five listed pins are 3.3 V only.
- Flashing: DFU via BOOT + RESET, or a web programmer; debugging with an ST-Link V3 Mini (recommended in the getting-started guide).
- Software: libDaisy and DaisySP in C++; the datasheet also lists Arduino and Max/MSP Gen~. Default audio block 48 samples at 48 kHz.

### B: Teensy 4.1 + audio adaptor Rev D2

Sources: PJRC Teensy 4.1 page; PJRC audio adaptor page; Teensy Audio Library source.

- Arm Cortex-M7 at 600 MHz; 1,024 KB RAM (512 KB tightly coupled); 7,936 KB flash; pads for extra PSRAM or flash chips.
- 55 I/O pins (42 breadboard-accessible); 18 analogue inputs (10-bit default, "only up to 10 bits are normally usable due to noise"); 8 serial, 3 SPI, 3 I2C, 2 I2S/TDM ports.
- Pins are 3.3 V and not 5 V tolerant; recommended maximum output current 4 mA.
- USB device port (with class-compliant USB MIDI and USB audio options) and a separate USB host port.
- Audio adaptor: SGTL5000 codec, 16-bit 44.1 kHz; headphone and line out; line in or mic in; controlled over I2C.
- Audio Library default: 128-sample blocks at 44.1 kHz, 16-bit integer processing.
- Flashing: Teensy Loader via the Arduino IDE with the Teensy boards add-on (Teensyduino), PlatformIO or Makefiles; recovery via the Program button. PJRC does not document a probe-based debugging header.
- Revision notes: PJRC's page lists component changes for boards made after 2022 (for example, the bootloader chip U2 became a GD32E230F8 from June 2022), so record when your board was made.
- PJRC's pages note that SparkFun now manufactures Teensy products.

### C: Raspberry Pi 5 + DAC+

Sources: Raspberry Pi 5 product brief; Raspberry Pi audio boards documentation.

- Quad-core Arm Cortex-A76 at 2.4 GHz; 1–16 GB RAM options; 4 USB ports; 40-pin GPIO header; 5 V / 5 A USB-C power.
- No analogue audio output: the product brief lists none, and Raspberry Pi's model list shows a 3.5 mm audio/AV jack for earlier models but not for Pi 5. A HAT or USB interface is needed.
- DAC+: TI PCM5122, 24-bit 192 kHz, line out 0–2 V RMS on phono sockets, headphone amplifier; output only (the Codec Zero adds inputs).
- HATs are auto-detected from an on-board EEPROM, or configured with a device-tree overlay; audio runs through Linux.
- GPIO pins are 3.3 V digital I/O (Raspberry Pi's GPIO documentation describes them only as high/low inputs and outputs, with no ADC), so knobs need an external ADC chip.
- Production stated until at least January 2036 (product brief).

## Step 4: tabulate, and mark gaps honestly

| Criterion | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audio out | Line, 1 V RMS | Line + phones | 0–2 V RMS line |
| Audio in | Yes | Yes | No (DAC+) |
| Knob inputs | 12 ADC | 18 ADC | External ADC |
| Debug probe | ST-Link (SWD) | Not documented | Linux tools |
| Boot | Firmware | Firmware | Linux OS |
| Block default | 48 @ 48k | 128 @ 44.1k | Configurable |

Then list what the official sources **do not** tell you, and how you will find out:

- **Real CPU headroom for your synth.** Clock speeds are not workloads. Estimate from an offline prototype, then measure on the board (lesson 6).
- **Boot time** of the Linux configuration. Measure it.
- **Noise and output quality** in your studio. Listen and record.
- **Cost.** Prices change; record them on the day you buy, including shipping, headers, cables, a MIDI circuit and any probe.
- **Compatibility with your other equipment.** Check the Digitakt and audio interface manuals for ports and levels. A USB connector alone proves nothing: two USB *devices* cannot talk to each other directly; one side must be a host.

## Step 5: score, then test the scoring

Apply must-haves as pass/fail first. Then score the survivors on each weighted criterion, with a sentence of evidence per score. Then check whether the result depends on your weights.

```python
# Placeholder scores (1-5), NOT real data.
scores = {
    "X": {"audio": 4, "debug": 4,
          "docs": 3},
    "Y": {"audio": 3, "debug": 2,
          "docs": 5},
}

def rank(weights):
    total = {
        name: sum(weights[c] * s[c]
                  for c in weights)
        for name, s in scores.items()
    }
    return sorted(total.items(),
                  key=lambda kv: -kv[1])

print(rank({"audio": 3, "debug": 2,
            "docs": 1}))
print(rank({"audio": 1, "debug": 1,
            "docs": 3}))
```

```
[('X', 23), ('Y', 18)]
[('Y', 20), ('X', 17)]
```

Same scores, different weights, opposite winner. That is the point of the exercise: a weighted matrix makes your priorities explicit. If a small, defensible change of weights flips the result, the options are close, and the deciding factor should be a test, not arithmetic.

## Step 6: run the smallest decisive experiment

Before committing, try the cheapest experiment that could change your mind:

- Run your oscillator and filter code offline on the computer and count operations per sample, to estimate CPU need.
- If one board is already available, do the roadmap's stage-6 exercises: flash and recover, read a knob and button, pass audio, measure load.
- Prototype the MIDI input circuit on a breadboard from the specification, at low voltage.

## Step 7: record the decision

Write a decision record (the project has `docs/decisions/` for this) containing:

1. The criteria and weights, with reasons.
2. The exact configurations, revisions and sources, with check dates.
3. The evidence table, including gaps and how they were closed.
4. The decision, the runner-up, and what would make you revisit it.
5. A parts list with compatibility checks, produced before purchase.

## Common mistakes

- **Comparing headline numbers.** 600 MHz versus 480 MHz says little about whether your synth fits; memory placement, library efficiency and your own code matter more.
- **Forgetting the rest of the system.** The board is a fraction of the build: MIDI circuit, power, connectors and enclosure all count.
- **Trusting a forum post or an old video.** Use the official page for the exact revision, then verify on the bench.
- **Choosing for the final instrument only.** The project also values learning. A platform that hides the codec teaches less about integration but gets you to sound sooner. Decide which you want for version 1.

> [!note] Content absent pending reliable verification
> A project-specific wiring diagram, compatible bill of materials, measured voice count and end-to-end latency are not supplied here: the project has not selected its board, controls or exact interface, and no hardware bench measurements are available. Generic examples cannot reliably establish those facts. Confirm the configuration and measure it before treating any example as a build specification.

## Key takeaways
- Write criteria and weights from the project before reading spec sheets; separate must-haves from scored criteria.
- Compare exact configurations (board, revision, audio board, MIDI circuit, power, tools), not product families.
- Use only official sources, record model, revision, URL and date, and re-verify before buying.
- Mark gaps explicitly; close the important ones with measurements, not assumptions.
- Test the sensitivity of a weighted score; if small weight changes flip the result, run an experiment.

## Further reading
- [Daisy Seed hardware page — Electro-Smith](https://docs.daisy.audio/hardware/Seed/)
- [Daisy Seed datasheet v1.2.0 — Electro-Smith](https://daisy.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/products/seed/Daisy_Seed_datasheet.pdf)
- [Teensy 4.1 — PJRC](https://www.pjrc.com/store/teensy41.html)
- [Audio adaptor boards for Teensy — PJRC](https://www.pjrc.com/store/teensy3_audio.html)
- [Teensy Audio Library — PJRC](https://www.pjrc.com/teensy/td_libs_Audio.html)
- [Raspberry Pi 5 product brief — Raspberry Pi](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rpi5/raspberry-pi-5-product-brief.pdf)
- [Raspberry Pi audio boards overview — Raspberry Pi documentation source](https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/accessories/audio/introduction.adoc)
- [Raspberry Pi audio boards configuration — Raspberry Pi documentation source](https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/accessories/audio/configuration.adoc)
- [GPIO on Raspberry Pi — Raspberry Pi documentation source](https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/computers/raspberry-pi/gpio-on-raspberry-pi.adoc)
- [Raspberry Pi models and their ports (Pi 5 lists no 3.5 mm jack) — Raspberry Pi documentation source](https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/computers/raspberry-pi/introduction.adoc)

questions.prompt: According to the lesson's method, what should you do *before* reading any board's spec sheet?

options.text: Sort the candidates by CPU clock speed
options.explanation: Starting from the biggest numbers is exactly the bias the method avoids; clock speed is not workload.

options.text: Write down the project's criteria, split into must-haves and weighted criteria, with weights and reasons
options.explanation: Correct. Criteria come from the project brief and hardware checklist, so the comparison measures fitness for this project.

options.text: Buy the cheapest board to try it
options.explanation: The roadmap says not to buy the main board merely to complete an early exercise, and to research compatibility before buying.

options.text: Read forum recommendations
options.explanation: Forum posts can help find questions to ask, but the method relies on official sources and your own criteria.

questions.workedExample:
Order of work:

1. Criteria and weights (from the project).
2. Exact configurations.
3. Official evidence with dates.
4. Table plus gaps.
5. Score and test sensitivity.
6. Smallest decisive experiment.
7. Decision record.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson insist on recording the model *revision* and the date checked for every product fact?

options.text: Because hardware details change between revisions (the Daisy Seed has used three different codecs) and documentation is updated, so an undated fact may no longer be true
options.explanation: Correct. Revisions change parts, and pages change. A dated, revision-specific fact can be re-checked.

options.text: It is a legal requirement for hobby projects
options.explanation: There is no such requirement; it is good engineering practice for reproducibility.

options.text: Because prices are listed by revision
options.explanation: Prices change independently of revision; this is about technical facts.

options.text: Revisions only affect the board's colour
options.explanation: Daisy Seed revisions changed the audio codec: a significant electrical change.

questions.workedExample:
Daisy Seed datasheet v1.2.0:

| Rev | Codec |
|---|---|
| 4 | AK4556 |
| 5 | WM8731 |
| 7 | PCM3060 |

A note saying 'Daisy uses a WM8731' is only true for Rev 5. Recording revision plus date makes the claim checkable.

questions.prompt: You plan 10 knobs. Using only the official documentation summarised in the lesson, which configuration needs an extra chip just to read knobs at all?

options.text: Daisy Seed Rev 7
options.explanation: It has 12 ADC inputs, enough for 10 knobs directly.

options.text: Teensy 4.1
options.explanation: It has 18 analogue inputs.

options.text: None of them
options.explanation: One of them has no analogue inputs on its GPIO header.

options.text: Raspberry Pi 5 with the DAC+
options.explanation: Correct. Raspberry Pi's GPIO documentation describes the 40-pin header as 3.3 V digital inputs and outputs, with no analogue inputs, so an external ADC chip is required.

questions.workedExample:
Count ADC inputs:

```
Daisy Seed  12 -> fits 10
Teensy 4.1  18 -> fits 10
Pi 5         0 -> needs ADC
```

That external ADC adds parts, wiring and driver work, which belongs in the cost and effort columns.

questions.prompt: Your synth must also process an external audio input (for example a filter for the Digitakt's output). Which of the three example configurations fails this must-have as specified?

options.text: Daisy Seed Rev 7
options.explanation: The Seed has stereo audio inputs via its codec.

options.text: Raspberry Pi 5 + DAC+
options.explanation: Correct. The DAC+ is output only (line out and headphones). The Codec Zero, a different Raspberry Pi audio board, adds inputs, which would be a different configuration.

options.text: Teensy 4.1 + audio adaptor
options.explanation: The adaptor offers stereo line-in or mono mic input.

options.text: All three fail
options.explanation: Two of the three have inputs.

questions.workedExample:
Check the inputs row against the sources:

- Daisy Seed: audio in, 3.6 Vpp AC coupled.
- Teensy adaptor: line in or mic.
- Pi DAC+: features table lists line out and headphones only.

A must-have failure eliminates the configuration, but you can define a new one (Pi 5 + Codec Zero) and evaluate it separately.

questions.prompt: A spreadsheet shows Teensy 4.1 at 600 MHz and Daisy Seed at 480 MHz, and concludes "Teensy can run 25% more voices". What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.text: Nothing; voices scale exactly with clock speed
options.explanation: They do not. Memory placement, caches, library overheads, sample format and block size all affect cost per voice.

options.text: The Daisy is actually faster because it has more SDRAM
options.explanation: More SDRAM gives capacity (long delays, samples), not more computation per second.

options.text: Clock rate is not workload: the libraries, sample formats (16-bit int vs float), block sizes and memory placement differ, so you must measure your own code on each
options.explanation: Correct. The Teensy Audio Library uses 16-bit integer blocks of 128 samples; libDaisy hands float blocks of 48 by default. Only measurement of your synth answers the question.

options.text: Clock speeds are not published officially
options.explanation: Both manufacturers publish them; the issue is what they mean.

questions.workedExample:
600 / 480 = 1.25 is a ratio of clock rates, not of synth voices. Different factors per platform:

- Library format: int16 vs float.
- Block size: 128 vs 48 (per-call overhead).
- Memory: where code and data sit.

Estimate offline, then measure with a cycle counter on each.

questions.prompt: With placeholder scores X = {audio 4, debug 4, docs 3} and Y = {audio 3, debug 2, docs 5}, compute the weighted totals for weights audio 1, debug 1, docs 3.

options.explanation: Those are the totals for the *other* weighting (audio 3, debug 2, docs 1).
That is the unweighted sum of scores; the weights were not applied.
The totals are swapped between X and Y.
Correct. X: 4 + 4 + 9 = 17. Y: 3 + 2 + 15 = 20. Y wins under this weighting.

questions.workedExample:
```
X = 1*4 + 1*4 + 3*3
  = 4 + 4 + 9 = 17
Y = 1*3 + 1*2 + 3*5
  = 3 + 2 + 15 = 20
```

Under audio 3 / debug 2 / docs 1, X wins 23 to 18. The winner depends on the weights, which is why you justify them first.

questions.prompt: Which items belong in the cost and effort of a configuration, beyond the main board? Select all that apply.

options.text: The audio board or codec, if not on the main board
options.explanation: Correct. Teensy needs the audio adaptor; the Pi needs a HAT for analogue audio.

options.text: A DIN MIDI interface circuit built to the specification
options.explanation: Correct. None of the three boards has DIN MIDI jacks; the circuit and connectors are extra.

options.text: Power supply, cables, headers and any debug probe
options.explanation: Correct. The Daisy debug workflow uses an ST-Link; the Pi 5 needs a suitable 5 V supply.

options.text: The Ableton licence, which differs per board
options.explanation: Ableton is already part of the studio and does not change with the synth's board, so it does not distinguish the options.

questions.workedExample:
Build a per-configuration list:

```
board + audio board
+ MIDI circuit, jacks
+ power, cables, headers
+ probe/tools
+ shipping
```

Record prices on the purchase date; the lesson deliberately quotes none.

questions.prompt: You want the Digitakt to play the synth over USB. The synth board can act as a USB MIDI *device*. The Digitakt's USB port is also designed to connect to a computer. What must you verify?

options.text: Nothing; matching USB connectors mean they will work
options.explanation: The roadmap warns that a USB connector is not proof of compatibility. Roles matter.

options.text: That the cable is USB 3.0
options.explanation: Cable speed does not create a host where there is none.

options.text: Whether either device can act as a USB host; two devices cannot talk directly, so you may need a host (such as a board with a host port) or DIN MIDI instead
options.explanation: Correct. USB communication needs one host. Check the Digitakt manual for its USB role, and the board's docs (for example Teensy 4.1's separate host port).

options.text: That both run at 31,250 baud
options.explanation: That is DIN MIDI's UART rate; USB MIDI does not use it.

questions.workedExample:
USB is asymmetric: a host (usually a computer) and devices.

1. Synth board: device (USB MIDI).
2. Digitakt: check its manual for host support.
3. If neither is a host: use DIN MIDI, a board with a USB host port, or a USB MIDI host adapter.

Record the manual version and check date.

questions.prompt: Two configurations score 82 and 79. Changing one weight by a single point (which you can defend either way) reverses the order. What does the method recommend?

options.text: Pick the one with 82; the matrix has decided
options.explanation: A three-point margin that flips with a defensible tweak is noise, not a decision.

options.text: Treat them as tied on paper and run the smallest experiment that could separate them on the criterion that matters most
options.explanation: Correct. When scores are sensitive to weights, evidence beats arithmetic; for example, measure CPU load of a prototype voice, or test the debugging workflow.

options.text: Add more criteria until one wins clearly
options.explanation: Adding criteria after the fact lets bias pick the winner.

options.text: Choose the cheaper one automatically
options.explanation: Cost is one criterion among several, already in the matrix.

questions.workedExample:
Sensitivity test:

1. Vary each weight by ±1.
2. If the winner changes, the result is not robust.
3. Identify the criterion driving the flip.
4. Get real evidence for it (a measurement or a short trial).
5. Record both the scores and the experiment in the decision record.

questions.prompt: Which statements are supported by the official sources as checked on 2026-10-04? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teensy 4.1 digital pins are not 5 V tolerant
options.explanation: Correct. PJRC: 'The pins are not 5V tolerant. Do not drive any digital pin higher than 3.3V.'

options.text: The Teensy audio adaptor works at 24-bit 96 kHz by default
options.explanation: PJRC describes the adaptor as 16-bit, 44.1 kHz.

options.text: The Daisy Seed Rev 7 codec is a PCM3060 configured in hardware mode, not over I2C
options.explanation: Correct. The datasheet's codec page says so.

options.text: The Raspberry Pi DAC+ line output is 0–2 V RMS
options.explanation: Correct. Raspberry Pi's audio documentation gives this for the DAC+ phono outputs.

questions.workedExample:
Check each against its source:

| Claim | Source | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| T4.1 not 5 V tolerant | PJRC | True |
| Adaptor 24/96 | PJRC: 16/44.1 | False |
| Seed PCM3060 HW mode | Datasheet | True |
| DAC+ 0–2 V RMS | Pi docs | True |

Re-run this check before buying.

questions.prompt: The project values learning C++, DSP and embedded integration, and also wants a first instrument that is achievable. How should that tension show up in the comparison?

options.text: Ignore learning goals; only the finished instrument matters
options.explanation: The project brief lists learning as a confirmed goal, so it belongs in the criteria.

options.text: Always choose the platform that hides the most hardware detail
options.explanation: That maximises speed to sound but may under-serve the integration learning goal. It is a trade-off to weigh, not a rule.

options.text: Always choose a bare MCU plus separate codec to maximise learning
options.explanation: That maximises integration learning but risks an unachievable first build. Again a trade-off, not a rule.

options.text: Make 'fit with learning goals' and 'effort to first sound' explicit weighted criteria, decide their weights for version 1, and record that the balance may change for later versions
options.explanation: Correct. Making the tension explicit keeps it from being decided by accident, and versioning lets you revisit it.

questions.workedExample:
Two criteria pull in opposite directions:

- Effort to first sound: integrated audio boards score higher.
- Integration learning: separate codecs teach more.

Weight them deliberately for version 1, note the reasoning, and plan to revisit after the first build.
